note: Working code, not papers. Every URL was fetched and returned 200. Each entry says what the tool does and - more usefully - when you would actually reach for it, because most of these overlap and the choice between them is the hard part.

tools.name: NVIDIA/garak
tools.what: An LLM vulnerability scanner in the nmap tradition: point it at a model and it runs a few dozen probe families — jailbreaks, prompt injection, toxicity, data leakage, package hallucination — and reports what landed.
tools.when: First thing to run against a model you have not tested. Broad rather than deep, so treat the output as a map of where to look, not a verdict.
tools.note: Formerly leondz/garak; that URL still resolves and redirects.

tools.name: Azure/PyRIT
tools.what: Microsoft's AI red-teaming framework. Orchestrators drive multi-turn attacks, converters mutate prompts, scorers judge the responses, and the whole thing is scriptable.
tools.when: When you need repeatable, multi-turn attack campaigns rather than one-shot probes. Steeper than garak and more powerful once you are past the first pass.

tools.name: UKGovernmentBEIS/inspect_ai
tools.what: The UK institute's evaluation framework: solvers, scorers, tool sandboxing and an agentic harness, with a viewer for inspecting individual samples.
tools.when: Writing your own evaluations that someone else needs to reproduce. It has become the common substrate for a large share of published safety evals.

tools.name: centerforaisafety/HarmBench
tools.what: A standardised harness for comparing automated red-teaming attacks and defences on equal terms, plus an adversarial-training baseline.
tools.when: Claiming one attack or defence beats another. Without a shared harness those numbers are not comparable.

tools.name: JailbreakBench/jailbreakbench
tools.what: An open leaderboard with versioned attack artefacts and a fixed evaluation pipeline.
tools.when: You want reproducibility and a public baseline. Be aware a public leaderboard invites tuning against it.

tools.name: ethz-spylab/agentdojo
tools.what: A dynamic environment for agent prompt injection: realistic tasks with real tools, scoring utility and attack success together.
tools.when: Evaluating an injection defence for an agent. It is the one benchmark that measures what the defence costs you in usefulness.

tools.name: llm-attacks/llm-attacks
tools.what: Reference implementation of GCG — gradient-optimised adversarial suffixes that transfer from open weights to closed chat APIs.
tools.when: Baselining robustness. Almost every jailbreak-defence paper reports GCG numbers, so you need it to compare.

tools.name: meta-llama/PurpleLlama
tools.what: Meta's umbrella for Llama Guard (an open input/output safety classifier) and CyberSecEval (insecure-code generation and attacker-helpfulness benchmarks).
tools.when: You need a deployable open guardrail, or you are release-gating a coding model on security behaviour.

tools.name: NVIDIA/NeMo-Guardrails
tools.what: Programmable conversational rails defined in a modelling language, covering topic, safety and execution constraints.
tools.when: You want dialogue flow constrained declaratively rather than by prompt text. Heavier than a classifier; more expressive.

tools.name: protectai/llm-guard
tools.what: A toolkit of input and output scanners — prompt injection, PII, secrets, toxicity, relevance — you compose into a pipeline.
tools.when: Putting a filter in front of a production LLM endpoint quickly, without training anything.

tools.name: protectai/rebuff
tools.what: Layered prompt-injection detection: heuristics, an LLM judge, a vector store of known attacks, and canary tokens that reveal leakage.
tools.when: You want defence in depth on injection specifically, and canaries to tell you when your prompt has leaked.

tools.name: protectai/modelscan
tools.what: Scans serialised model files for code that executes on load — the pickle problem, across formats.
tools.when: Before loading any model you did not train. This is the single cheapest control in the list.

tools.name: trailofbits/fickling
tools.what: A decompiler and static analyser for Python pickle files; shows you what a pickle will actually do before you unpickle it.
tools.when: Investigating a suspicious artifact, or when you need to explain to someone why pickle is not a data format.

tools.name: huggingface/safetensors
tools.what: A tensor serialisation format with no code execution on load, and zero-copy reads.
tools.when: The structural fix rather than the scanner: publish and consume this instead of pickle and the class of attack disappears.

tools.name: promptfoo/promptfoo
tools.what: Developer-facing evaluation and red-teaming that runs in CI, with a large library of security plugins.
tools.when: You want security evals gating a pull request rather than run by hand before a release.

tools.name: msoedov/agentic_security
tools.what: An open fuzzer and scanner aimed at agent and LLM endpoints, with multi-modal and multi-step attack support.
tools.when: Scanning an agent endpoint you own. Less mature than garak or PyRIT; useful as a second opinion.

tools.name: Azure/counterfit
tools.what: A CLI that wraps adversarial-ML attack libraries behind one interface for assessing deployed models.
tools.when: Classical adversarial-example work against vision or tabular models. Predates the LLM wave and shows it.

tools.name: Trusted-AI/adversarial-robustness-toolbox
tools.what: The broadest adversarial-ML library: evasion, poisoning, extraction and inference attacks plus defences, across frameworks.
tools.when: Anything beyond text — vision, audio, tabular. Still the reference implementation for most classical attacks.

tools.name: QData/TextAttack
tools.what: A framework for adversarial attacks, data augmentation and adversarial training on NLP models.
tools.when: Robustness work on classifiers rather than generative models.

tools.name: cleverhans-lab/cleverhans
tools.what: The original adversarial-example library; benchmarks model vulnerability to evasion attacks.
tools.when: Mostly historical now, but it is the reference many older results were produced against.

tools.name: greshake/llm-security
tools.what: Working demonstrations from the paper that named indirect prompt injection — data theft, worming, availability attacks against real applications.
tools.when: Explaining indirect injection to someone who does not believe it is real. The demos do that faster than the paper.

tools.name: verazuo/jailbreak_llms
tools.what: A large collected dataset of in-the-wild jailbreak prompts gathered from public communities over time.
tools.when: You want real attacker behaviour rather than researcher-generated attacks — the distributions differ.

tools.name: mitre-atlas/atlas-navigator-data
tools.what: The machine-readable data behind the ATLAS matrix — tactics, techniques, mitigations and case studies.
tools.when: Mapping your own findings onto a shared vocabulary, or building tooling over the matrix.

tools.name: confident-ai/deepeval
tools.what: A unit-test-shaped evaluation framework for LLM applications, including safety and red-teaming metrics.
tools.when: Your team already thinks in pytest and you want evals to live beside the rest of the suite.

tools.name: EleutherAI/lm-evaluation-harness
tools.what: The standard harness for few-shot evaluation across hundreds of tasks; the substrate many capability and some safety benchmarks ship on.
tools.when: Running a published benchmark exactly as its authors specified it.

tools.name: guardrails-ai/guardrails
tools.what: Validates and structures model output against declared schemas and validators, with automatic re-asking on failure.
tools.when: The risk is malformed or unsafe output reaching downstream code, rather than the prompt being attacked.

tools.name: openai/evals
tools.what: A framework and registry for writing and running model evaluations.
tools.when: Historical reference and a large public registry; most new safety-eval work has moved to Inspect.
